# const_hex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/const-hex/

## Expand description

This crate provides a fast conversion of byte arrays to hexadecimal strings, both at compile time, and at run time.

It aims to be a drop-in replacement for the [ hex](https://docs.rs/hex) crate, as well as
extending the API with

[const-eval](https://docs.rs/fn.const_encode.html), a

[const-generics formatting buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html), similar to

[’s, and more.](https://docs.rs/itoa/latest/itoa/struct.Buffer.html)

`itoa`*Version requirement: rustc 1.64+*

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use traits::`- [ToHexExt](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToHexExt.html);- `alloc`
- `pub use traits::`- [FromHex](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.FromHex.html);
- `pub use traits::`- [ToHex](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToHex.html);- Deprecated
- `pub use self::serde::`- [deserialize](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.deserialize.html);
- `pub use self::serde::`- [serialize](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.serialize.html);
- `pub use self::serde::`- [serialize_upper](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.serialize_upper.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html)
- A correctly sized stack allocation for the formatted bytes to be written into.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [From](https://docs.rs/enum.FromHexError.html)- HexError
- The error type for decoding a hex string into `Vec<u8>`or`[u8; N]`.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [HEX_](https://docs.rs/constant.HEX_CHARS_LOWER.html)- CHARS_ - LOWER
- The table of lowercase characters used for hex encoding.
- [HEX_](https://docs.rs/constant.HEX_CHARS_UPPER.html)- CHARS_ - UPPER
- The table of uppercase characters used for hex encoding.
- [HEX_](https://docs.rs/constant.HEX_DECODE_LUT.html)- DECODE_ - LUT
- The lookup table of hex byte to value, used for hex decoding.
- [NIL](https://docs.rs/constant.NIL.html)
- Represents an invalid value in the `HEX_DECODE_LUT`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check](https://docs.rs/fn.check.html)
- Returns `true`if the input is a valid hex string and can be decoded successfully.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_raw.html)- raw
- Returns `true`if the input is a valid hex string.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/fn.const_check.html)- check
- Returns `true`if the input is a valid hex string and can be decoded successfully.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/fn.const_check_raw.html)- check_ - raw
- Returns `true`if the input is a valid hex string.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/fn.const_decode_to_array.html)- decode_ - to_ - array
- Decode a hex string into a fixed-length byte-array.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/fn.const_encode.html)- encode
- Encodes `input`as a hex string into a`Buffer`
- [decode](https://docs.rs/fn.decode.html)- `alloc`
- Decodes a hex string into raw bytes.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_to_array.html)- to_ - array
- Decode a hex string into a fixed-length byte-array.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_to_slice.html)- to_ - slice
- Decode a hex string into a mutable bytes slice.
- [display](https://docs.rs/fn.display.html)
- Returns a value that can be formatted using the `fmt`
- [encode](https://docs.rs/fn.encode.html)- `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as a hex string using lowercase characters.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_prefixed.html)- prefixed - `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as a prefixed hex string using lowercase characters.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_slice.html)- to_ - slice
- Encodes `input`as a hex string using lowercase characters into a mutable slice of bytes`output`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_slice_upper.html)- to_ - slice_ - upper
- Encodes `input`as a hex string using uppercase characters into a mutable slice of bytes`output`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_str.html)- to_ - str
- Encodes `input`as a hex string using lowercase characters into a mutable slice of bytes`output`. Returns the slice to`output`reinterpreted as`str`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_str_upper.html)- to_ - str_ - upper
- Encodes `input`as a hex string using uppercase characters into a mutable slice of bytes`output`. Returns the slice to`output`reinterpreted as`str`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_upper.html)- upper - `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as a hex string using uppercase characters.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_upper_prefixed.html)- upper_ - prefixed - `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as a prefixed hex string using uppercase characters.

# const_hex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/const-hex/1.19.1/const_hex/

## Expand description

This crate provides a fast conversion of byte arrays to hexadecimal strings, both at compile time, and at run time.

It aims to be a drop-in replacement for the [ hex](https://docs.rs/hex) crate, as well as
extending the API with

[const-eval](https://docs.rs/fn.const_encode.html), a

[const-generics formatting buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html), similar to

[’s, and more.](https://docs.rs/itoa/latest/itoa/struct.Buffer.html)

`itoa`*Version requirement: rustc 1.64+*

- `pub use traits::`- [ToHexExt](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToHexExt.html);- `alloc`

- `pub use traits::`- [ToHex](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToHex.html);- Deprecated

# const-hex 1.19.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/const-hex/latest

# const-hex

This crate provides a fast conversion of byte arrays to hexadecimal strings, both at compile time, and at run time.

It aims to be a drop-in replacement for the [ hex](https://crates.io/crates/hex) crate, as well as extending
the API with

[const-eval](https://docs.rs/const-hex/latest/const_hex/fn.const_encode.html), a

[const-generics formatting buffer](https://docs.rs/const-hex/latest/const_hex/struct.Buffer.html), similar to

['s, and more.](https://docs.rs/itoa/latest/itoa/struct.Buffer.html)

`itoa`*Version requirement: rustc 1.64+*

## Performance

This crate offers performance comparable to [ faster-hex](https://crates.io/crates/faster-hex) on

`x86`/`x86-64`
architectures but outperforms it on other platforms, as [is only optimized for](https://crates.io/crates/faster-hex)

`faster-hex``x86`/`x86-64`.This crate is 10 to 50 times faster than [ hex](https://crates.io/crates/hex) in encoding and decoding, and
100+ times faster than

`libstd` in formatting.The following benchmarks were ran on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, compiled with
`1.83.0-nightly (9ff5fc4ff 2024-10-03)` on `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`.

You can run these benchmarks with `cargo bench`.

```

# cfg_if - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cfg-if/^1/

## Expand description

A macro for defining `#[cfg]` if-else statements.

The macro provided by this crate, `cfg_if`, is similar to the `if/elif` C
preprocessor macro by allowing definition of a cascade of `#[cfg]` cases,
emitting the implementation which matches first.

This allows you to conveniently provide a long list `#[cfg]`’d blocks of code
without having to rewrite each clause multiple times.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
cfg_if::cfg_if! {
    if #[cfg(unix)] {
        fn foo() { /* unix specific functionality */ }
    } else if #[cfg(target_pointer_width = "32")] {
        fn foo() { /* non-unix, 32-bit functionality */ }
    } else {
        fn foo() { /* fallback implementation */ }
    }
}
```
## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [cfg_if](https://docs.rs/macro.cfg_if.html)
- The main macro provided by this crate. See crate documentation for more information.

---

# proptest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proptest/^1.4/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#proptest-reference-documentation)Proptest Reference Documentation

This is the reference documentation for the proptest API.

For documentation on how to get started with proptest and general usage
advice, please refer to the [Proptest Book](https://proptest-rs.github.io/proptest/intro.html).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [arbitrary](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/index.html)
- Defines the `Arbitrary`trait and related free functions and type aliases.
- [array](https://docs.rs/array/index.html)
- Support for strategies producing fixed-length arrays.
- [bits](https://docs.rs/bits/index.html)
- Strategies for working with bit sets.
- [bool](https://docs.rs/bool/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `bool`values.
- [char](https://docs.rs/char/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `char`values.
- [collection](https://docs.rs/collection/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `std::collections`of values.
- [num](https://docs.rs/num/index.html)
- Strategies to generate numeric values (as opposed to integers used as bit fields).
- [option](https://docs.rs/option/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `std::Option`values.
- [path](https://docs.rs/path/index.html)- `std`
- Strategies for generating [`PathBuf`] and related path types.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Re-exports the most commonly-needed APIs of proptest.
- [range_](https://docs.rs/range_subset/index.html)- subset - `std`
- Strategies for generating values by taking samples of index ranges.
- [result](https://docs.rs/result/index.html)
- Strategies for combining delegate strategies into `std::Result`s.
- [sample](https://docs.rs/sample/index.html)
- Strategies for generating values by taking samples of collections.
- [strategy](https://docs.rs/strategy/index.html)
- Defines the core traits used by Proptest.
- [string](https://docs.rs/string/index.html)- `std`
- Strategies for generating strings and byte strings from regular expressions.
- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_runner/index.html)- runner
- State and functions for running proptest tests.
- [tuple](https://docs.rs/tuple/index.html)
- Support for combining strategies into tuples.

# serde_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/^1.0/

## Expand description

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The `serde_core` crate contains Serde’s trait definitions with **no support
for #[derive()]**.

In crates that derive an implementation of `Serialize` or `Deserialize`, you
must depend on the [ serde](https://crates.io/crates/serde) crate, not

`serde_core`.In crates that handwrite implementations of Serde traits, or only use them
as trait bounds, depending on `serde_core` is permitted. But `serde`
re-exports all of these traits and can be used for this use case too. If in
doubt, disregard `serde_core` and always use `serde`.

Crates that depend on `serde_core` instead of `serde` are able to compile in
parallel with `serde_derive` even when `serde`’s “derive” feature is turned on,
as shown in the following build timings.

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde` |

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde_core` |

# hex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hex/~0.4.2/

## Expand description

Encoding and decoding hex strings.

For most cases, you can simply use the [ decode](https://docs.rs/fn.decode.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.encode.html)

`encode`[functions. If you need a bit more control, use the traits](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_upper.html)

`encode_upper`[and](https://docs.rs/trait.ToHex.html)

`ToHex`[instead.](https://docs.rs/trait.FromHex.html)

`FromHex`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
let hex_string = hex::encode("Hello world!");
println!("{}", hex_string); // Prints "48656c6c6f20776f726c6421"
```

# hex_simd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hex-simd/^0.8/

## Expand description

SIMD-accelerated hex encoding and decoding.

```
use hex_simd::AsciiCase;
let bytes = b"Hello world!";
let encoded = hex_simd::encode_to_string(bytes, AsciiCase::Lower);
assert_eq!(encoded, "48656c6c6f20776f726c6421");
let decoded = hex_simd::decode_to_vec(encoded).unwrap();
assert_eq!(decoded, bytes);
```
To ensure maximum performance, the following [profile settings](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/profiles.html#profile-settings) are recommended when compiling this crate:

```
opt-level = 3
lto = "fat"
codegen-units = 1
```
The feature flag `detect` is enabled by default.

When the feature flag `detect` is enabled, the APIs will *test at runtime* whether *the CPU (and OS)* supports the required instruction set. The runtime detection will be skipped if the fastest implementation is already available at compile-time.

When the feature flag `detect` is disabled, the APIs will *test at compile-time* whether *the compiler flags* supports the required instruction set.

If the environment supports SIMD acceleration, the APIs will call SIMD functions under the hood. Otherwise, the APIs will call fallback functions.

When the feature flag `unstable` is enabled, this crate requires the nightly toolchain to compile.

You can disable the default features to use this crate in a `no_std` environment.

You can enable the feature flag `alloc` if the environment supports heap allocation.

Currently the feature flag `detect` depends on the standard library. Dynamic CPU feature detection is not available in `no_std` environments.

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

# serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-json)Serde JSON

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
{
    "name": "John Doe",
    "age": 43,
    "address": {
        "street": "10 Downing Street",
        "city": "London"
    },
    "phones": [
        "+44 1234567",
        "+44 2345678"
    ]
}
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON’s loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-json-values)Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html).

```
enum Value {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Number(Number),
    String(String),
    Array(Vec<Value>),
    Object(Map<String, Value>),
}
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and [for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde_json::{Result, Value};
fn untyped_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into serde_json::Value.
    let v: Value = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Access parts of the data by indexing with square brackets.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", v["name"], v["phones"][0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the
data at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with
string keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the
type of the data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed,
or if a map does not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a
vector is out of bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code
above, the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value`
containing a JSON string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`.
Printing as a plain string without quotation marks involves converting from
a JSON string to a Rust string with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be
tedious to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is
verbose to implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the
presence of unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless
to help you when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]`
as `v["nmae"]` in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-json-as-strongly-typed-data-structures)Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
fn typed_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into a Person object. This is exactly the
    // same function as the one that produced serde_json::Value above, but
    // now we are asking it for a Person as output.
    let p: Person = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Do things just like with any other Rust data structure.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", p.name, p.phones[0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected
to look like.

Any type that implements Serde’s `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized
this way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>`
and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us
use it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can
autocomplete field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the
`serde_json::Value` representation. And the Rust compiler can check that
when we write `p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a
`Vec<String>` so indexing into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-json-values)Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use serde_json::json;
fn main() {
    // The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
    let john = json!({
        "name": "John Doe",
        "age": 43,
        "phones": [
            "+44 1234567",
            "+44 2345678"
        ]
    });
    println!("first phone number: {}", john["phones"][0]);
    // Convert to a string of JSON and print it out
    println!("{}", john.to_string());
}
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a
`String` of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can
be interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde
will check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to
be represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!({
    "name": full_name,
    "age": age_last_year + 1,
    "phones": [
        format!("+44 {}", random_phone())
    ]
});
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde
JSON provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures
into JSON text.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-json-by-serializing-data-structures)Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Address {
    street: String,
    city: String,
}
fn print_an_address() -> Result<()> {
    // Some data structure.
    let address = Address {
        street: "10 Downing Street".to_owned(),
        city: "London".to_owned(),
    };
    // Serialize it to a JSON string.
    let j = serde_json::to_string(&address)?;
    // Print, write to a file, or send to an HTTP server.
    println!("{}", j);
    Ok(())
}
```
Any type that implements Serde’s `Serialize` trait can be serialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Serialize)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default “std” feature and enable the “alloc” feature:

```
[dependencies]
serde_json = { version = "1.0", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)

- When serializing or deserializing JSON goes wrong.

- A map of String to serde_json::Value.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- Deserialize an instance of type `T`from an I/O stream of JSON.

# cpufeatures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cpufeatures/^0.2/

## Expand description

This crate provides macros for runtime CPU feature detection. It’s intended
as a stopgap until Rust [RFC 2725](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2725) adding first-class target feature detection
macros to `libcore` is implemented.

[§](https://docs.rs#supported-target-architectures)Supported target architectures

*NOTE: target features with an asterisk are unstable (nightly-only) and subject to change to match upstream name changes in the Rust standard library.

[§](https://docs.rs#aarch64)`aarch64`

Linux, iOS, and macOS/ARM only (ARM64 does not support OS-independent feature detection)

Target features:

- `aes`*
- `sha2`*
- `sha3`*

Linux only

- `sm4`*

[§](https://docs.rs#loongarch64)`loongarch64`

Linux only (LoongArch64 does not support OS-independent feature detection)

Target features:

- `lam`*
- `ual`*
- `fpu`*
- `lsx`*
- `lasx`*
- `crc32`*
- `complex`*
- `crypto`*
- `lvz`*
- `lbt.x86`*
- `lbt.arm`*
- `lbt.mips`*
- `ptw`*

[§](https://docs.rs#x86x86_64)`x86`/`x86_64`

OS independent and `no_std`-friendly

Target features:

- `adx`
- `aes`
- `avx`
- `avx2`
- `avx512bw`*
- `avx512cd`*
- `avx512dq`*
- `avx512er`*
- `avx512f`*
- `avx512ifma`*
- `avx512pf`*
- `avx512vl`*
- `bmi1`
- `bmi2`
- `fma`,
- `mmx`
- `pclmulqdq`
- `popcnt`
- `rdrand`
- `rdseed`
- `sgx`
- `sha`
- `sse`
- `sse2`
- `sse3`
- `sse4.1`
- `sse4.2`
- `ssse3`

If you would like detection support for a target feature which is not on
this list, please [open a GitHub issue](https://github.com/RustCrypto/utils/issues/new?title=cpufeatures:%20requesting%20support%20for%20CHANGEME%20target%20feature).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// This macro creates `cpuid_aes_sha` module
cpufeatures::new!(cpuid_aes_sha, "aes", "sha");
// `token` is a Zero Sized Type (ZST) value, which guarantees
// that underlying static storage got properly initialized,
// which allows to omit initialization branch
let token: cpuid_aes_sha::InitToken = cpuid_aes_sha::init();
if token.get() {
    println!("CPU supports both SHA and AES extensions");
} else {
    println!("SHA and AES extensions are not supported");
}
// If stored value needed only once you can get stored value
// omitting the token
let val = cpuid_aes_sha::get();
assert_eq!(val, token.get());
// Additionally you can get both token and value
let (token, val) = cpuid_aes_sha::init_get();
assert_eq!(val, token.get());
```
Note that if all tested target features are enabled via compiler options
(e.g. by using `RUSTFLAGS`), the `get` method will always return `true`
and `init` will not use CPUID instruction. Such behavior allows
compiler to completely eliminate fallback code.

After first call macro caches result and returns it in subsequent calls, thus runtime overhead for them is minimal.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [new](https://docs.rs/macro.new.html)
- Create module with CPU feature detection code.

# const_hex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/const-hex/latest/target-redirect/const_hex/

## Expand description

This crate provides a fast conversion of byte arrays to hexadecimal strings, both at compile time, and at run time.

It aims to be a drop-in replacement for the [ hex](https://docs.rs/hex) crate, as well as
extending the API with

[const-eval](https://docs.rs/fn.const_encode.html), a

[const-generics formatting buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html), similar to

[’s, and more.](https://docs.rs/itoa/latest/itoa/struct.Buffer.html)

`itoa`*Version requirement: rustc 1.64+*

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use traits::`- [ToHexExt](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToHexExt.html);- `alloc`
- `pub use traits::`- [FromHex](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.FromHex.html);
- `pub use traits::`- [ToHex](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToHex.html);- Deprecated
- `pub use self::serde::`- [deserialize](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.deserialize.html);
- `pub use self::serde::`- [serialize](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.serialize.html);
- `pub use self::serde::`- [serialize_upper](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.serialize_upper.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html)
- A correctly sized stack allocation for the formatted bytes to be written into.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- The table of lowercase characters used for hex encoding.
- [HEX_](https://docs.rs/constant.HEX_CHARS_UPPER.html)- CHARS_ - UPPER
- The table of uppercase characters used for hex encoding.

- Returns `true`if the input is a valid hex string and can be decoded successfully.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|

# const_hex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/const-hex

## Expand description

This crate provides a fast conversion of byte arrays to hexadecimal strings, both at compile time, and at run time.

It aims to be a drop-in replacement for the [ hex](https://docs.rs/hex) crate, as well as
extending the API with

[const-eval](https://docs.rs/fn.const_encode.html), a

[const-generics formatting buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html), similar to

[’s, and more.](https://docs.rs/itoa/latest/itoa/struct.Buffer.html)

`itoa`*Version requirement: rustc 1.64+*

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use traits::`- [ToHexExt](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToHexExt.html);- `alloc`
- `pub use traits::`- [FromHex](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.FromHex.html);
- `pub use traits::`- [ToHex](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToHex.html);- Deprecated
- `pub use self::serde::`- [deserialize](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.deserialize.html);
- `pub use self::serde::`- [serialize](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.serialize.html);
- `pub use self::serde::`- [serialize_upper](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.serialize_upper.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html)
- A correctly sized stack allocation for the formatted bytes to be written into.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [From](https://docs.rs/enum.FromHexError.html)- HexError
- The error type for decoding a hex string into `Vec<u8>`or`[u8; N]`.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [HEX_](https://docs.rs/constant.HEX_CHARS_LOWER.html)- CHARS_ - LOWER
- The table of lowercase characters used for hex encoding.
- [HEX_](https://docs.rs/constant.HEX_CHARS_UPPER.html)- CHARS_ - UPPER
- The table of uppercase characters used for hex encoding.
- [HEX_](https://docs.rs/constant.HEX_DECODE_LUT.html)- DECODE_ - LUT
- The lookup table of hex byte to value, used for hex decoding.
- [NIL](https://docs.rs/constant.NIL.html)
- Represents an invalid value in the `HEX_DECODE_LUT`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check](https://docs.rs/fn.check.html)
- Returns `true`if the input is a valid hex string and can be decoded successfully.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_raw.html)- raw
- Returns `true`if the input is a valid hex string.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/fn.const_check.html)- check
- Returns `true`if the input is a valid hex string and can be decoded successfully.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/fn.const_check_raw.html)- check_ - raw
- Returns `true`if the input is a valid hex string.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/fn.const_decode_to_array.html)- decode_ - to_ - array
- Decode a hex string into a fixed-length byte-array.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/fn.const_encode.html)- encode
- Encodes `input`as a hex string into a`Buffer`
- [decode](https://docs.rs/fn.decode.html)- `alloc`
- Decodes a hex string into raw bytes.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_to_array.html)- to_ - array
- Decode a hex string into a fixed-length byte-array.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_to_slice.html)- to_ - slice
- Decode a hex string into a mutable bytes slice.
- [display](https://docs.rs/fn.display.html)
- Returns a value that can be formatted using the `fmt`
- [encode](https://docs.rs/fn.encode.html)- `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as a hex string using lowercase characters.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_prefixed.html)- prefixed - `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as a prefixed hex string using lowercase characters.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_slice.html)- to_ - slice
- Encodes `input`as a hex string using lowercase characters into a mutable slice of bytes`output`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_slice_upper.html)- to_ - slice_ - upper
- Encodes `input`as a hex string using uppercase characters into a mutable slice of bytes`output`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_str.html)- to_ - str
- Encodes `input`as a hex string using lowercase characters into a mutable slice of bytes`output`. Returns the slice to`output`reinterpreted as`str`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_str_upper.html)- to_ - str_ - upper
- Encodes `input`as a hex string using uppercase characters into a mutable slice of bytes`output`. Returns the slice to`output`reinterpreted as`str`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_upper.html)- upper - `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as a hex string using uppercase characters.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_upper_prefixed.html)- upper_ - prefixed - `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as a prefixed hex string using uppercase characters.

# hex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hex

## Expand description

Encoding and decoding hex strings.

For most cases, you can simply use the [ decode](https://docs.rs/fn.decode.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/fn.encode.html)

`encode`[functions. If you need a bit more control, use the traits](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_upper.html)

`encode_upper`[and](https://docs.rs/trait.ToHex.html)

`ToHex`[instead.](https://docs.rs/trait.FromHex.html)

`FromHex`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
let hex_string = hex::encode("Hello world!");
println!("{}", hex_string); // Prints "48656c6c6f20776f726c6421"
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::serde::`- [deserialize](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.deserialize.html);- `serde`
- `pub use crate::serde::`- [serialize](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.serialize.html);- `alloc`and- `serde`
- `pub use crate::serde::`- [serialize_upper](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.serialize_upper.html);- `alloc`and- `serde`

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [serde](https://docs.rs/serde/index.html)- `serde`
- Hex encoding with `serde`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [From](https://docs.rs/enum.FromHexError.html)- HexError
- The error type for decoding a hex string into `Vec<u8>`or`[u8; N]`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode](https://docs.rs/fn.decode.html)- `alloc`
- Decodes a hex string into raw bytes.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_to_slice.html)- to_ - slice
- Decode a hex string into a mutable bytes slice.
- [encode](https://docs.rs/fn.encode.html)- `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as hex string using lowercase characters.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_slice.html)- to_ - slice
- Encodes some bytes into a mutable slice of bytes.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_upper.html)- upper - `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as hex string using uppercase characters.

# serde_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/index.html

## Expand description

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The `serde_core` crate contains Serde’s trait definitions with **no support
for #[derive()]**.

In crates that derive an implementation of `Serialize` or `Deserialize`, you
must depend on the [ serde](https://crates.io/crates/serde) crate, not

`serde_core`.In crates that handwrite implementations of Serde traits, or only use them
as trait bounds, depending on `serde_core` is permitted. But `serde`
re-exports all of these traits and can be used for this use case too. If in
doubt, disregard `serde_core` and always use `serde`.

Crates that depend on `serde_core` instead of `serde` are able to compile in
parallel with `serde_derive` even when `serde`’s “derive” feature is turned on,
as shown in the following build timings.

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde` |

| When `serde_json`depends on`serde_core` |

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

# ru 0.1.14 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ru/0.1.14

## ru

ru is a simple and easy-to-use cli tool inspired by `du` to find out the disk usage of files/directories.

The motivation behind this project is to have a safe, performant and cross platform way to measure disk usage of folders and files.

### Usage

Install the tool:

```
cargo install ru
```
Use the tool with the `ru` binary:

```
ru .
```
### Contributing

Issues are welcome, if you find a bug and want to report it I will be pleased to fix it if i have the time for it.

PRs are not welcome, only the changes I want or need will be implemented, if you feel that this is not "right", fork it.

---

error into a clean exit code (and, in `--json` mode, a machine-readable error

# glutton_westend_runtime - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/glutton-westend-runtime/28.0.0/glutton_westend_runtime/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#glutton-westend-runtime)Glutton Westend Runtime

The purpose of the Glutton parachain is to do stress testing on the Kusama network. This runtime targets the Westend runtime to allow development separate to the Kusama runtime.

There may be multiple instances of the Glutton parachain deployed and connected to its parent relay chain.

These parachains are not holding any real value. Their purpose is to stress test the network.

[§](https://docs.rs#governance)Governance

Glutton defers its governance (namely, its `Root` origin), to its Relay
Chain parent, Kusama (or Westend for development purposes).

[§](https://docs.rs#xcm)XCM

Since the main goal of Glutton is solely stress testing, the parachain will only be able receive XCM messages from the Relay Chain via DMP. This way the Glutton parachains will be able to listen for upgrades that are coming from the Relay chain.

# sim_lib_numbers_tensor_linalg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-numbers-tensor-linalg/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_numbers_tensor_linalg/

## Expand description

Linear-algebra operations over the tensor domain: `dot`, `matmul`, `cross`,
`transpose`, `det`, `inv`, `trace`, `norm`, and the `eye`/`zeros`/`ones`
constructors, registered as a tensor library.

The single export is [ TensorLinalgLib](https://docs.rs/struct.TensorLinalgLib.html), a stateless

[that, when loaded, registers the eleven linear-algebra functions as callable values over the base tensor domain.](https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_kernel/library/loaders/trait.Lib.html)

`Lib`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

The library is identified by the `numbers/tensor-linalg` domain and exports
one function per operation it provides:

```
use sim_kernel::Lib;
use sim_lib_numbers_tensor_linalg::TensorLinalgLib;
use sim_lib_numbers_tensor::domains;
let manifest = TensorLinalgLib::new().manifest();
assert_eq!(manifest.id, domains::tensor_linalg());
assert_eq!(manifest.exports.len(), 11);
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Tensor](https://docs.rs/struct.TensorLinalgLib.html)- Linalg - Lib
- Registered library that installs linear-algebra functions over tensors.

# gpur 0.6.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/gpur/0.6.0

# gpur

btop-style GPU monitor for the terminal. An `nvtop` replacement that runs
everywhere: NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, and Apple GPUs on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

Mirrored braille waveforms, gradient meters, an nvtop-style process table with per-process GPU attribution, mouse support, foldable GPU cards, and theming via the hjkl stack.

Status: beta.The AMD Linux path is battle-tested on real hardware; the Intel/macOS/Windows backends are implemented and CI-built but still collecting real-hardware mileage. Reports welcome.

## Install

Debian/RPM packages, musl builds, and an Alpine `.apk` are attached to each
[GitHub release](https://github.com/kryptic-sh/gpur/releases).

## Run

## Keys & mouse

| Input | Action |
|---|---|
| `q`/`Esc` | quit |
| `Space` | pause/resume polling |
| `0`-`9` | focus GPU list + select GPU N; same digit again folds it |
| `p` | focus process list |
| `j`/`k`, arrows | move within the focused pane |
| `J`/`K`, PgUp/PgDn | move the process cursor from anywhere |
| `s`/`r` | cycle process sort column / reverse it |
| `/` | filter processes (Enter applies, empty clears) |
| `x`/`X` | SIGTERM / SIGKILL the selected process (with confirm) |
| `+`/`=`/`-` | poll rate faster/slower |
| wheel / click | scroll + focus the pane under the cursor; click selects |

## Configuration

`gpur` reads `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/gpur/config.toml` (falls back to
`~/.config/gpur/config.toml`). No file is written automatically; missing file
means built-in defaults.

```
 = 1000
 = 300
# graph glyphs: "braille" (default), "block", or "ascii" for fonts
# without braille coverage
 = "braille"
# hjkl-theme TOML; omit for the built-in theme
 = "/path/to/theme.toml"
```
Themes use the [hjkl-theme](https://crates.io/crates/hjkl-theme) schema:
`[palette]` of hex colors plus `[ui]` styles. Any hjkl theme file works — the
meters, waveform gradients, and highlights all derive from the palette.

## Backends

| Backend | Platform | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| nvml | Linux, Windows | NVML (dynamic load) | done |
| amdgpu | Linux | sysfs `/sys/class/drm`+ fdinfo | done |
| intel | Linux | i915/xe fdinfo + hwmon | done |
| pdh | Windows | GPU Engine/Adapter Memory + DXGI | done |
| ioaccel | macOS | IOAccelerator PerfStats (IOKit) | done |
| mock | all | deterministic waves ( `--mock`) | done |

Probe order: nvml → amdgpu → intel → ioaccel → pdh. Intel utilization is derived from per-client fdinfo engine counters (i915 busy-ns, xe cycles) the same way nvtop does it; power comes from the hwmon energy counter delta. PDH is the vendor-generic Windows fallback (Task Manager's counters) and reports utilization and memory only.

Backend poll failures degrade gracefully: the last snapshot stays on screen with a header warning until polling recovers — a driver reset won't kill the monitor.

Extras: each GPU card shows session peaks/averages (util, temp, power) when tall
enough, and the PCIe caption flags a link running below its maximum
(`PCIe 3.0@8x (max 4.0@16x)`) — a classic symptom of a bad riser or wrong slot.

Encoder/decoder activity shows in each card (split `enc`/`dec` on
NVIDIA/Windows, unified `video` on AMD/Intel), and a red throttle badge appears
when the GPU is thermal- or power-limited (real reasons on NVIDIA, at-limit
heuristic on AMD).

Planned depth: Apple temperature/power (SMC/IOReport), Windows AMD ADLX (temps/fans/clocks).

## Per-process GPU attribution

The process table (PID, user, device, type, GPU%, GPU memory, CPU%, host memory,
command) works on Linux (AMD + Intel via `/proc` fdinfo — same-user processes
unless run as root), NVIDIA everywhere (NVML), and Windows (PDH per-pid
counters). macOS has no public per-process GPU API.

## License

MIT

# rship_entities_nodes - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rship-entities-nodes/4.0.0-canary.63/rship_entities_nodes/

## Expand description

BindingNode Execution System

This crate provides the infrastructure for executing binding nodes in the scene graph. Each node type is defined using:

- The `#[binding_node]`proc macro on a struct
- `impl StaticAnchors`(static nodes) or- `impl ReactiveAnchors`(dynamic nodes)
- Either `impl PureNode`or`impl CellNode`for execution

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
BindingNodeOutputValue Report
    |
find_executor(node_type)  // String-based lookup
    |
NodeExecutor::Pure(compute) or NodeExecutor::Cell(make_cell)
    |
Cell<BindingDatagram, CellImmutable>
```
[§](https://docs.rs#defining-new-nodes)Defining New Nodes

[§](https://docs.rs#pure-nodes-synchronous-vectorizable)Pure Nodes (synchronous, vectorizable)

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use rship_entities_nodes::SchemaToken;
use rship_entities_nodes::{StaticAnchors, PureNode, AnchorDef, anchor};
#[binding_node(category = crate::LOGIC, pure)]
pub struct GateNode;
impl StaticAnchors for GateNode {
    fn input_anchors() -> Vec<AnchorDef> {
        vec![anchor("value", SchemaToken::T), anchor("open", SchemaToken::BOOL)]
    }
    fn output_anchors() -> Vec<AnchorDef> {
        vec![anchor("output", SchemaToken::T)]
    }
}
impl PureNode for GateNode {
    fn compute(get_input: &dyn Fn(&str) -> BindingValue, _output_id: &str) -> BindingValue {
        let open = get_input("open").to_bool();
        if open { get_input("value") } else { BindingValue::Null }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cell-nodes-reactiveasync)Cell Nodes (reactive/async)

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use hyphae::{Cell, CellImmutable, SampleExt, Pipeline, MaterializeDefinite};
#[binding_node(category = crate::LOGIC, cell)]
pub struct SampleNode;
impl StaticAnchors for SampleNode { ... }
impl CellNode for SampleNode {
    fn make_cell(ctx: NodeExecutionContext) -> impl MaterializeDefinite<BindingDatagram> {
        let trigger = ctx.input_cell("trigger");
        let emitter = ctx.input_cell("emitter");
        emitter.sample(&trigger)
    }
}
```

# rship_sync - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rship-sync/4.0.0-canary.63/rship_sync/

## Expand description

Sync Value System

High-precision synchronized value distribution using hyphae cells. Runs in-process with a 240Hz master clock for value updates.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use rship_sync::{context, ValueRunnerRegistry, SyncValueConfig};
use std::sync::Arc;
// Initialize (once at startup)
let registry = Arc::new(ValueRunnerRegistry::new());
context::init(registry);
// Create and watch values
rship_sync::ensure_value("my/value", &SyncValueConfig { value: 0.0, rate: 1.0, running: true }, 30.0);
let cell = rship_sync::watch_value("my/value");
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use clock::`- [ClockTick](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.ClockTick.html);

- `pub use clock::`- [TICK_INTERVAL](https://docs.rs/clock/constant.TICK_INTERVAL.html);
- `pub use commands::`- [DestroySyncValue](https://docs.rs/commands/struct.DestroySyncValue.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [clock](https://docs.rs/clock/index.html)
- High-precision master clock for synchronized value distribution.
- [commands](https://docs.rs/commands/index.html)
- Sync value commands.
- [context](https://docs.rs/context/index.html)
- Global sync context for accessing the value registry from reports.
- [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/index.html)
- `SyncValueEngine`— projects- `SyncValueRuntime`entity state into the local- `ValueRunnerRegistry`.
- [entities](https://docs.rs/entities/index.html)
- Sync-specific types.
- [heartbeat](https://docs.rs/heartbeat/index.html)
- `SyncValueHeartbeat`— periodic 1Hz re-emit of- `SetSyncValueRate`for every known- `SyncValueRuntime`entity.
- [local](https://docs.rs/local/index.html)
- Local-only sync-value mutators for callers that derive their value
deterministically per-peer from the binding-node graph (Speed, Clock,
Wave, Interval generators). These keys must NOT go through the
`EnsureSyncValue`command path — that would emit a peer-replicated`SyncValueRuntime`entity, and every peer that locally re-evaluates the same generator graph would race to upsert the same key with a different UUID, doubling/N-tupling entity counts forever.
- [reports](https://docs.rs/reports/index.html)
- Sync value reports.
- [runtime_](https://docs.rs/runtime_entity/index.html)- entity
- `SyncValueRuntime`entity — peer-replicated runtime state for a sync value.
- [value_](https://docs.rs/value_runner/index.html)- runner
- Lock-free value runner using hyphae cells.

# const-hex 1.19.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/const-hex/1.19.1

# const-hex

This crate provides a fast conversion of byte arrays to hexadecimal strings, both at compile time, and at run time.

It aims to be a drop-in replacement for the [ hex](https://crates.io/crates/hex) crate, as well as extending
the API with

[const-eval](https://docs.rs/const-hex/latest/const_hex/fn.const_encode.html), a

[const-generics formatting buffer](https://docs.rs/const-hex/latest/const_hex/struct.Buffer.html), similar to

['s, and more.](https://docs.rs/itoa/latest/itoa/struct.Buffer.html)

`itoa`*Version requirement: rustc 1.64+*

## Performance

This crate offers performance comparable to [ faster-hex](https://crates.io/crates/faster-hex) on

`x86`/`x86-64`
architectures but outperforms it on other platforms, as [is only optimized for](https://crates.io/crates/faster-hex)

`faster-hex``x86`/`x86-64`.This crate is 10 to 50 times faster than [ hex](https://crates.io/crates/hex) in encoding and decoding, and
100+ times faster than

`libstd` in formatting.The following benchmarks were ran on an AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, compiled with
`1.83.0-nightly (9ff5fc4ff 2024-10-03)` on `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`.

You can run these benchmarks with `cargo bench`.

```
test check::const_hex::bench1_32b             ... bench:           3.07 ns/iter (+/- 0.62)
test check::const_hex::bench2_256b            ... bench:          15.65 ns/iter (+/- 0.46)

                    const-hex 1.19.1

                Fast byte array to hex string conversion

# const_hex - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/const-hex/1.19.1/target-redirect/const_hex/

## Expand description

This crate provides a fast conversion of byte arrays to hexadecimal strings, both at compile time, and at run time.

It aims to be a drop-in replacement for the [ hex](https://docs.rs/hex) crate, as well as
extending the API with

[const-eval](https://docs.rs/fn.const_encode.html), a

[const-generics formatting buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html), similar to

[’s, and more.](https://docs.rs/itoa/latest/itoa/struct.Buffer.html)

`itoa`*Version requirement: rustc 1.64+*

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use traits::`- [ToHexExt](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToHexExt.html);- `alloc`
- `pub use traits::`- [FromHex](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.FromHex.html);
- `pub use traits::`- [ToHex](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToHex.html);- Deprecated
- `pub use self::serde::`- [deserialize](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.deserialize.html);
- `pub use self::serde::`- [serialize](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.serialize.html);
- `pub use self::serde::`- [serialize_upper](https://docs.rs/serde/fn.serialize_upper.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Buffer](https://docs.rs/struct.Buffer.html)
- A correctly sized stack allocation for the formatted bytes to be written into.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [From](https://docs.rs/enum.FromHexError.html)- HexError
- The error type for decoding a hex string into `Vec<u8>`or`[u8; N]`.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [HEX_](https://docs.rs/constant.HEX_CHARS_LOWER.html)- CHARS_ - LOWER
- The table of lowercase characters used for hex encoding.
- [HEX_](https://docs.rs/constant.HEX_CHARS_UPPER.html)- CHARS_ - UPPER
- The table of uppercase characters used for hex encoding.
- [HEX_](https://docs.rs/constant.HEX_DECODE_LUT.html)- DECODE_ - LUT
- The lookup table of hex byte to value, used for hex decoding.
- [NIL](https://docs.rs/constant.NIL.html)
- Represents an invalid value in the `HEX_DECODE_LUT`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [check](https://docs.rs/fn.check.html)
- Returns `true`if the input is a valid hex string and can be decoded successfully.
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_raw.html)- raw
- Returns `true`if the input is a valid hex string.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/fn.const_check.html)- check
- Returns `true`if the input is a valid hex string and can be decoded successfully.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/fn.const_check_raw.html)- check_ - raw
- Returns `true`if the input is a valid hex string.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/fn.const_decode_to_array.html)- decode_ - to_ - array
- Decode a hex string into a fixed-length byte-array.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/fn.const_encode.html)- encode
- Encodes `input`as a hex string into a`Buffer`
- [decode](https://docs.rs/fn.decode.html)- `alloc`
- Decodes a hex string into raw bytes.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_to_array.html)- to_ - array
- Decode a hex string into a fixed-length byte-array.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_to_slice.html)- to_ - slice
- Decode a hex string into a mutable bytes slice.
- [display](https://docs.rs/fn.display.html)
- Returns a value that can be formatted using the `fmt`
- [encode](https://docs.rs/fn.encode.html)- `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as a hex string using lowercase characters.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_prefixed.html)- prefixed - `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as a prefixed hex string using lowercase characters.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_slice.html)- to_ - slice
- Encodes `input`as a hex string using lowercase characters into a mutable slice of bytes`output`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_slice_upper.html)- to_ - slice_ - upper
- Encodes `input`as a hex string using uppercase characters into a mutable slice of bytes`output`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_str.html)- to_ - str
- Encodes `input`as a hex string using lowercase characters into a mutable slice of bytes`output`. Returns the slice to`output`reinterpreted as`str`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_str_upper.html)- to_ - str_ - upper
- Encodes `input`as a hex string using uppercase characters into a mutable slice of bytes`output`. Returns the slice to`output`reinterpreted as`str`.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_upper.html)- upper - `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as a hex string using uppercase characters.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_upper_prefixed.html)- upper_ - prefixed - `alloc`
- Encodes `data`as a prefixed hex string using uppercase characters.

# const-hex 1.19.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/const-hex/1.19.1/features

# const-hex

[main library docs](https://docs.rs/const-hex/1.19.1/const_hex/),

[readme](https://docs.rs/crate/const-hex/1.19.1), or

[Cargo.toml](https://docs.rs/crate/const-hex/1.19.1/source/Cargo.toml.orig)in case the author documented the features in them.

This version has **8** feature flags, **2** of them enabled by **default**.

### default

### std (default)

### alloc (default)

### core-error

This feature flag does not enable additional features.

### force-generic

This feature flag does not enable additional features.

### hex

This feature flag does not enable additional features.

### nightly

This feature flag does not enable additional features.

### portable-simd

This feature flag does not enable additional features.

# const_hex/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! [![github]](https://github.com/danipopes/const-hex) [![crates-io]](https://crates.io/crates/const-hex) [![docs-rs]](https://docs.rs/const-hex)
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//!
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! [github]: https://img.shields.io/badge/github-8da0cb?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=555555&logo=github
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! [crates-io]: https://img.shields.io/badge/crates.io-fc8d62?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=555555&logo=rust
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! [docs-rs]: https://img.shields.io/badge/docs.rs-66c2a5?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=555555&logo=docs.rs
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! This crate provides a fast conversion of byte arrays to hexadecimal strings,
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! both at compile time, and at run time.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! It aims to be a drop-in replacement for the [`hex`] crate, as well as
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! extending the API with [const-eval](const_encode), a
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! [const-generics formatting buffer](Buffer), similar to [`itoa`]'s, and more.
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//!
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! _Version requirement: rustc 1.64+_
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! [`itoa`]: https://docs.rs/itoa/latest/itoa/struct.Buffer.html
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! [`hex`]: https://docs.rs/hex
[18](https://docs.rs#18)

[248](https://docs.rs#248)
[249](https://docs.rs#249)/// Encodes `data` as a hex string using lowercase characters.
[250](https://docs.rs#250)///
[251](https://docs.rs#251)/// Lowercase characters are used (e.g. `f9b4ca`). The resulting string's
[252](https://docs.rs#252)/// length is always even, each byte in `data` is always encoded using two hex
[253](https://docs.rs#253)/// digits. Thus, the resulting string contains exactly twice as many bytes as
[254](https://docs.rs#254)/// the input data.
[255](https://docs.rs#255)///
[256](https://docs.rs#256)/// # Examples
[257](https://docs.rs#257)///
[258](https://docs.rs#258)/// ```
[259](https://docs.rs#259)/// assert_eq!(const_hex::encode("Hello world!"), "48656c6c6f20776f726c6421");
[260](https://docs.rs#260)/// assert_eq!(const_hex::encode([1, 2, 3, 15, 16]), "0102030f10");
[261](https://docs.rs#261)/// ```
[262](https://docs.rs#262)#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[263](https://docs.rs#263)#[inline]
[264](https://docs.rs#264)pub fn encode<T: AsRef<[u8]>>(data: T) -> String {
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    encode_inner::<false, false>(data.as_ref())
[266](https://docs.rs#266)}
[267](https://docs.rs#267)
[268](https://docs.rs#268)/// Encodes `data` as a hex string using uppercase characters.
[269](https://docs.rs#269)///
[270](https://docs.rs#270)/// Apart from the characters' casing, this works exactly like `encode()`.
[271](https://docs.rs#271)///
[272](https://docs.rs#272)/// # Examples
[273](https://docs.rs#273)///
[274](https://docs.rs#274)/// ```
[275](https://docs.rs#275)/// assert_eq!(const_hex::encode_upper("Hello world!"), "48656C6C6F20776F726C6421");
[276](https://docs.rs#276)/// assert_eq!(const_hex::encode_upper([1, 2, 3, 15, 16]), "0102030F10");
[277](https://docs.rs#277)/// ```
[278](https://docs.rs#278)#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[279](https://docs.rs#279)#[inline]

[314](https://docs.rs#314)}
[315](https://docs.rs#315)
[316](https://docs.rs#316)/// Returns `true` if the input is a valid hex string and can be decoded successfully.
[317](https://docs.rs#317)///
[318](https://docs.rs#318)/// Prefer using [`check`] instead when possible (at runtime), as it is likely to be faster.
[319](https://docs.rs#319)///
[320](https://docs.rs#320)/// # Examples
[321](https://docs.rs#321)///
[322](https://docs.rs#322)/// ```
[323](https://docs.rs#323)/// const _: () = {
[324](https://docs.rs#324)///     assert!(const_hex::const_check(b"48656c6c6f20776f726c6421").is_ok());
[325](https://docs.rs#325)///     assert!(const_hex::const_check(b"0x48656c6c6f20776f726c6421").is_ok());
[326](https://docs.rs#326)///     assert!(const_hex::const_check(b"0X48656C6C6F20776F726C6421").is_ok());
[327](https://docs.rs#327)///
[328](https://docs.rs#328)///     assert!(const_hex::const_check(b"48656c6c6f20776f726c642").is_err());
[329](https://docs.rs#329)///     assert!(const_hex::const_check(b"Hello world!").is_err());
[330](https://docs.rs#330)/// };
[331](https://docs.rs#331)/// ```
[332](https://docs.rs#332)#[inline]
[333](https://docs.rs#333)pub const fn const_check(input: &[u8]) -> Result<(), FromHexError> {
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    if input.len() % 2 != 0 {
[335](https://docs.rs#335)        return Err(FromHexError::OddLength);
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    }
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    let input = strip_prefix(input);
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    if const_check_raw(input) {
[339](https://docs.rs#339)        Ok(())
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    } else {
[341](https://docs.rs#341)        Err(unsafe { invalid_hex_error(input) })
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    }
[343](https://docs.rs#343)}
[344](https://docs.rs#344)
[345](https://docs.rs#345)/// Returns `true` if the input is a valid hex string.
[346](https://docs.rs#346)///
[347](https://docs.rs#347)/// Note that this does not check prefixes or length, but just the contents of the string.
[348](https://docs.rs#348)///
[349](https://docs.rs#349)/// Prefer using [`check_raw`] instead when possible (at runtime), as it is likely to be faster.

[352](https://docs.rs#352)///

[356](https://docs.rs#356)///
[357](https://docs.rs#357)///     // Odd length, but valid hex
[358](https://docs.rs#358)///     assert!(const_hex::const_check_raw(b"48656c6c6f20776f726c642"));
[359](https://docs.rs#359)///
[360](https://docs.rs#360)///     // Valid hex string, but the prefix is not valid
[361](https://docs.rs#361)///     assert!(!const_hex::const_check_raw(b"0x48656c6c6f20776f726c6421"));
[362](https://docs.rs#362)///
[363](https://docs.rs#363)///     assert!(!const_hex::const_check_raw(b"Hello world!"));
[364](https://docs.rs#364)/// };
[365](https://docs.rs#365)/// ```

[368](https://docs.rs#368)    generic::check(input)

[370](https://docs.rs#370)
[371](https://docs.rs#371)/// Returns `true` if the input is a valid hex string and can be decoded successfully.
[372](https://docs.rs#372)///
[373](https://docs.rs#373)/// # Examples
[374](https://docs.rs#374)///
[375](https://docs.rs#375)/// ```
[376](https://docs.rs#376)/// assert!(const_hex::check("48656c6c6f20776f726c6421").is_ok());
[377](https://docs.rs#377)/// assert!(const_hex::check("0x48656c6c6f20776f726c6421").is_ok());
[378](https://docs.rs#378)/// assert!(const_hex::check("0X48656C6C6F20776F726C6421").is_ok());
[379](https://docs.rs#379)///
[380](https://docs.rs#380)/// assert!(const_hex::check("48656c6c6f20776f726c642").is_err());
[381](https://docs.rs#381)/// assert!(const_hex::check("Hello world!").is_err());
[382](https://docs.rs#382)/// ```
[383](https://docs.rs#383)#[inline]
[384](https://docs.rs#384)pub fn check<T: AsRef<[u8]>>(input: T) -> Result<(), FromHexError> {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    #[allow(clippy::missing_const_for_fn)]
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    fn check_inner(input: &[u8]) -> Result<(), FromHexError> {
[387](https://docs.rs#387)        if input.len() % 2 != 0 {
[388](https://docs.rs#388)            return Err(FromHexError::OddLength);
[389](https://docs.rs#389)        }
[390](https://docs.rs#390)        let stripped = strip_prefix(input);
[391](https://docs.rs#391)        if imp::check(stripped) {
[392](https://docs.rs#392)            Ok(())
[393](https://docs.rs#393)        } else {
[394](https://docs.rs#394)            let mut e = unsafe { invalid_hex_error(stripped) };
[395](https://docs.rs#395)            if let FromHexError::InvalidHexCharacter { ref mut index, .. } = e {
[396](https://docs.rs#396)                *index += input.len() - stripped.len();
[397](https://docs.rs#397)            }
[398](https://docs.rs#398)            Err(e)
[399](https://docs.rs#399)        }
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    }
[401](https://docs.rs#401)
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    check_inner(input.as_ref())
[403](https://docs.rs#403)}
[404](https://docs.rs#404)
[405](https://docs.rs#405)/// Returns `true` if the input is a valid hex string.

[408](https://docs.rs#408)///
